title: Holidays in Taiwan
goal: Talk about Taiwan's holidays and customs — while building long descriptions with 的, the skill that opens the way to A2.
bekal: build long descriptions in front of a noun with 的
name Taiwan's holidays and what people do on them
give the right greeting for each holiday

dialogs.title: 對話 — 過年
dialogs.intro: With Lunar New Year approaching, Xiaomei invites Budi to dinner at her family's home.

notes: ⚠️ **紅包 are given only to people who aren't married** — children, teens, and single young adults. Once you marry, you switch from receiver to giver. It's a joke repeated endlessly in Taiwan.
**旺來 is Taiwanese Hokkien (台語), not Mandarin.** Pineapple in Taiwanese sounds like *ōng-lâi*, and *ōng* means "prosperous". Sound puns like this are at the heart of all Chinese good-luck customs.

**年夜飯 ("year-night meal") is the most important dinner of the year** — the night before Lunar New Year, when the whole family gathers. All of Taiwan stops; shops close, trains are packed, highways are jammed.
⚠️ **Being invited to a 年夜飯 is a great honor**, not small talk. Accept, bring fruit or cake, and be ready to eat far more than you think you can.

**台語 (Taiwanese Hokkien) is spoken at home by more than half of Taiwan's population**, especially in the south and among older people. It's a different language from Mandarin, not a dialect of it — but hundreds of its words have entered everyday Taiwanese Mandarin.

grammars.title: Long 的 phrases: building relative clauses
body: In unit 3 you used 的 for possession. Now it's time to use it for the job English does with **"who/which/that"** — and the difference is big: Mandarin puts the whole description **in front of** the noun.

head: 中文
Pīnyīn
Literally
Meaning
rows: a friend who works in Taipei

after: ⚠️ **Read it from the end.** English puts the noun first ("the book **that I bought**"); Mandarin puts it last. To read 我買的書, start from 書 (book), then go backward: the book *that* I bought.
**The noun can be dropped when it's obvious**: *我買的* = "the one I bought", *紅的* = "the red one", *最便宜的* = "the cheapest one". This form is used constantly when shopping.

**This is the skill that most clearly separates A1 from A2.** As long as you can only make short sentences, you sound like a textbook; once you can string descriptions together with 的, your sentences start to sound like a real person's.

grammars.title: Greetings and the 祝 pattern
body: Mandarin holiday greetings are almost all four characters long, and almost all of them can be preceded by **祝你…** ("I wish you…").
after: ⚠️ **Children often follow 恭喜發財 with 紅包拿來** ("hand over the red envelope") — jokingly. You can say it too with people you're close to; it's seen as funny, not rude.
**For older people, wishes about health are worth more than wishes about money**: 身體健康, 長命百歲 (may you live to a hundred).

blocks.text: ⚠️ **中秋節 in Taiwan has a custom found nowhere else: 烤肉 (barbecue).** The whole country grills meat on sidewalks, in parks, and outside their homes on the night of the full moon. The custom didn't even exist a hundred years ago — it was born from soy-sauce ads in the 1980s, and now it's inseparable from the holiday.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Four New Year taboos
items: **Don't sweep the floor on the first day** — sweeping outward is seen as throwing away the fortune that just came in.
**Don't break anything.** If you do, quickly say *歲歲平安* (*suìsuì píng'ān*) — a pun on 碎 (shatter), which sounds the same as 歲 (year).
**Don't say the words 死 (die), 病 (sick), or 輸 (lose)** during the holiday.
**Don't wear white or black** — those two colors are for mourning. Red is the right color.
⚠️ If you forget and break one of them, no one will be angry with you as a foreigner. But knowing them will impress your hosts.

sections.title: 拜拜: going to the temple

blocks.text: Taiwan has more than twelve thousand temples — more than convenience stores. Going to a temple isn't just for the very religious; ordinary people drop by before an exam, before a job interview, or simply in passing.

head: 中文
Pīnyīn
Meaning
rows: ⚠️ sea goddess, the most revered in Taiwan

blocks.text: ⚠️ **媽祖 is the protector goddess of seafarers and the most revered figure in Taiwanese folk religion.** The yearly 大甲媽祖 procession covers more than three hundred kilometers over nine days and draws hundreds of thousands of people — one of the largest religious processions in the world. Tourists are welcome to join and are fed for free along the way.
